Your first level as a spellcaster gives you 3 cantrips and 6 1st level spells. After each long rest, you can prepare spells equal to your spellcaster level plus your Intelligence Modifier, or 1 plus your Intelligence Modifier. You have 2 1st level spell slots to cast these spells. If you then take 3 levels in a martial class that allows spellcasting and choose a specific archetype that also uses Intelligence as the spellcasting ability and the same spell list, you will know 3 cantrips and 6 1st level spells from your initial class; and 2 cantrips and 3 1st level spells from the martial archetype, for a total of 5 cantrips and 9 first level spells. Of these spells, you always have the 3 archetype spells prepared, and you can prepare 1 plus your Intelligence Modifier spells from your initial class, for a total of 4 plus your Intelligence Modifier possible spells you can cast.

To determine your spell slots, you take your initial class levels and add your martial class levels divided by three and rounded down: Initial Class Levels + Martial Class Levels/3. In the case of a 1st level initial class and 3 levels in the martial class, you get 1 + 3/3 = 2. This is your total spellcaster level. A table in the core rulebook shows how many of each level of spell slots you have for all total spellcaster levels. In the case of a 1st level initial class and 3 levels in the martial class, you're a 2nd level spellcaster and as such you have 3 1st level spell slots.

So, as a 1st level initial class and 3 levels in the martial class, you have 5 cantrips, which you can use at will, and 4 plus your Intelligence Modifier spells prepared (3 archetype spells and 1 plus your Intelligence Modifier initial class spells), of which you can cast 3. If you continue leveling up in the martial class, you gain another cantrip when you reach a certain level, at which point you also know 7 archetype spells (for a total of 13 spells: 6 from your initial class and 7 from the martial class). When you are 1st level in your initial class and 10 levels in the martial class, your total spellcaster level is 1 + 10/3 = 4, and so you have 4 1st level spell slots and 3 2nd level spell slots. This also means that if you come across a 2nd level spell from your initial class, you can add it to your spellbook, prepare it, and cast it. The earliest level you have access to 2nd level spell slots is -assuming 1st level in your initial class and X levels in the martial class- at 1st level in your initial class and 6 levels in the martial class. At that point, you can learn 2nd level spells:

The Spells Known column of the martial archetype's spellcasting table shows when you learn more spells of 1st level or higher. Each of these spells must be an abjuration or evocation spell of your choice, and must be of a level for which you have spell slots.

Since you have 2nd level spell slots, you can learn 2nd level spells. Similarly, you can scribe 2nd level spells from your initial class in your spellbook.

As for ritual casting, your initial class gives you a feature that allows you to cast spells as a ritual. When spells are cast as a ritual, they consume no spell slot and are cast at the lowest level they can be cast. In order to cast a spell as a ritual, you have to have it prepared, or on your list of spells known, unless your ritual feature specifies differently, such as the one from your initial class. In the case of your initial class, you have to have the spell scribed in your spellbook. So this means that as a 1st level initial class and X levels in the martial class, you can cast any spell you know as a ritual, provided it has the ritual tag.

Infinite damage is impossible. Well, there might be one exception, but I'll save that for last. The reasons I can think of are threefold.

Firstly, there is the conceptual problem. Infinite isn't a number; it's a concept. You can't really work with it, since the normal arithmetic rules don't apply to infinity.

Secondly, the mathematical argument. I will simplify things to a four-sided die as an example, but the general idea applies to multiple dice and different types of dice as well. The chance of rolling maximum damage on a four-sided die is 1/4. The chance of rolling maximum damage again after already having rolled maximum damage is also 1/4, since it does not matter what your previous roll was. However, the chance of rolling maximum damage twice is (1/4)². For three times, it becomes (1/4)³, and for N times, it becomes (1/4)^N. If we now let N approach infinity, we will see that this value edges closer and closer to 0. So, assuming we could roll an infinite amount of times (which we can't because of the previous argument), the chance of rolling an infinite amount of damage is in fact 0.

Thirdly, there's the logistical argument. There is only so much time that A) you're alive, B) the session lasts, and C) the game master has patience. Even if you were to be incredibly lucky and reroll a lot of dice, at some point, the game master is going to step in to keep the game moving. In this case, the game master might rule infinite damage, but it doesn't matter; you defeated the opponent nonetheless.

Now, I mentioned there might be a situation where infinite damage could be feasible (assuming we ignore the first argument), and that is unarmed strikes. They do a flat 1 damage (if you aren't a specific type of character or don't have a certain feat), and as such, they always do maximum damage. If you consider this a roll with auto-maximum damage, then this would always result in infinite damage. This is because the a^N for N going to infinity goes to 0 only if the absolute value of a is less than 1. If |a|=1, it goes to 1, and if |a|>1, it goes to infinity. However, in-game, this raises the question of why anyone would pick up a weapon if punching someone could defeat them instantly. So, for that reason alone, it can and probably will be ruled that this is not the case.

For damaging spells, there are two types in general. Those that require an attack roll (like a fire-based spell or a necromantic spell...) where you roll an attack against the target's Armor Class. You would roll 1d20 plus your Proficiency Bonus plus your Intelligence Modifier (as a spellcaster, other classes have different spellcasting abilities). If the value you rolled equals or exceeds the target's Armor Class, you hit and then roll for damage. These are usually single-target spells, or multiple single-target ray spells (one spell targets one foe, while another has multiple rays that can target different foes or one foe).

The second type is typically for area of effect spells, such as a cone of fire, or enchantment-like spells, such as a command spell. In these cases, you roll for damage, and then the targets must make some sort of saving throw. Usually, this will be Dexterity, Constitution, or Wisdom. The spell's description specifies which. To determine whether they succeeded in saving and take half damage, or are unaffected, or whatever the outcome is when they save, they must exceed your spellcasting Difficulty Class. This is calculated as 8 plus your Proficiency Modifier plus your Intelligence Modifier (again, casters with different spellcasting abilities use that modifier for their Difficulty Class).

While it is waiting for the command to finally consume the wearer, or until he is weak enough, or whatever will trigger its appetite, the mimic armour sneaks off in the night to feed on rodents, birds, stray cats, and even small dogs on occasion. It exhibits this behaviour only after a few nights of observation. It needs to ensure that there is a set routine and get the timing right. It makes sure to never stray too far, so that when the wearer wakes up, the armour is still there. However, it will never be in quite the same location or position as where it was left. At first, the character(s) might not notice anything out of the ordinary, but after a while, it becomes strange as he starts to notice that some things are off. This behaviour will also interact curiously with spells like Alarm. The armour will almost certainly not be designated to not trigger the effect, making the caster paranoid: he keeps waking up from an intrusion, but never can he find one.

In settlements, this should pose no problem. Armour is removed at night, and the mimic can wander about 'freely', taking other shapes to avoid detection. It can feed on the inn's inevitable rodent problem and return in time for the wearer to wake up. But out in the wilderness, things can get a bit more complicated. Characters might sleep in their armour (in case those pesky creatures infesting the forest attack), and removing itself might prove troublesome for the armour. And if it does get free, it would be unfortunate if those pesky creatures do indeed attack. Then the fighter suddenly isn't wearing his armour, making him significantly more vulnerable. But it will also make him wonder what happened to it.

NOTE: I'm assuming a specific role-playing game system, because that's all I know.

EDIT: Casting a spell to identify it can also yield some interesting results. According to the rules, the caster learns what spells are affecting the creature they're touching, if any. Similarly, a spell to detect magic would show the caster that the armour is affected by transmutation magic. Combining these results should indicate to the caster that something is amiss. However, this can be circumvented by having the mimic be a lining in the armour. The armour itself is magical and will be identified correctly, but it will also conceal the mimic.

It takes a divine spellcaster, nature-based spellcaster, or holy warrior at least 1 minute of prayer or meditation, and an arcane spellcaster at least 1 minute of study per spell level for each spell on their list. For instance, a level 1 divine spellcaster wishing to prepare two level 1 spells would need to meditate for at least 2 minutes, whereas a level 20 divine spellcaster changing out all spells would need at least 89 minutes. The same applies to a nature-based spellcaster, holy warrior, or arcane spellcaster. All other classes that can cast have spells that they know at all times and can cast at all times.

Assuming the standard character sheet, as provided by a well-known game publisher, I would have the player list their known spells on the character sheet, and in the case of a divine spellcaster, nature-based spellcaster, holy warrior, or arcane spellcaster, have them mark if the spell is prepared. What spell slots you have are detailed in the player's handbook, in the table that lists the class features. A full caster (such as bards, divine spellcasters, nature-based spellcasters, sorcerers, and arcane spellcasters) can cast 2 level 1 spells at level 1, 3 level 1 spells at level 2, etc. Note that you can choose to cast one spell three times, or three spells once each, or one spell twice and another once at level 2. Also note that when you have access to higher level spell slots, you can cast lower level spells using one of the higher level slots. For example, you could cast a basic spell as a second level spell. Most of the time, this will increase the effectiveness of the spell. Half-casters (such as holy warriors and rangers) have a slower progression. They get their first spell slots at level 2 and gain access to second level spell slots at level 5, as opposed to full casters at level 3. Third-casters (such as certain martial spellcasters) have an even slower spell progression, gaining their first spell slots at level 3. Additionally, everyone who can cast cantrips can cast them whenever they wish, without spending a spell slot on them.

There are two ways Armor Class (AC) can be affected. The first is when it's a formula. For instance, normal AC without wearing any armor is 10 plus Dexterity modifier. A character of a certain class can add their Wisdom modifier, and another class can add their Constitution modifier (provided they don't wear armor). Another example is regular armor, which sets the AC at a specific value; heavy armor sets your AC at 18, medium armor at 15 plus Dexterity (maximum 2), and light armor at 12 plus Dexterity. Whenever such a thing (feat, item, spell...) is a 'formula', and you happen to have multiple sources (e.g., a character's unarmored defense and a protective spell), you pick either one of them, usually the higher.

The second type is an additive bonus. For instance, a shield adds +2 to your AC, regardless of other factors (not entirely sure how it affects unarmored defense). Similarly, a protective spell adds 5 to your AC for a short duration. Whenever a thing (feat, item, spell...) has an additive bonus, it gets added on top of the formula from the first point.

The way the probability works is that if you want outcome A from process 1 and outcome B from process 2, you multiply the odds of outcome A happening and the odds of outcome B happening. (Assuming process 1 doesn't influence process 2 and vice versa, but with two dice rolls, this isn't the case, and we can ignore this stipulation.) So let's say we flip a coin and roll a four-sided die. The odds of heads happening on the coin is 0.5, and the same for tails. Similarly, for a four-sided die, the odds of rolling a 1 is 0.25, and the same for the other numbers. Now we know that each possible outcome (H1, T1, H2, T2...) has a 1 in 8 chance of occurring: 0.5x0.25=0.125=1/8. If we assign a certain category, for instance, to each of these outcomes, we have even odds of every category happening. Now, if we want a certain category to occur more often, we can assign two outcomes, let's say H1 and H2. (Obviously, we'll lose one other category, but let's ignore that for now.) Now the odds of being in that category are 1/8+1/8=1/4, and the odds of other categories are still 1/8.

The same principle applies to a coin flip and a hundred-sided die roll. If you want some category to be half the population, you can say: flip a coin, if it's heads, you're [CATEGORY], if not, roll 1d100. If you want it to be 25%, or 30% you assign 1-25 (or 30) to that category, and say: flip a coin, if it's heads, roll on table A, if not, roll on table B. This will provide the same distribution as 1d200, which is not the same as 2d100. If you don't believe me, you can try it for yourself. Flip a coin and roll a six-sided die a hundred times. Tally how much of each outcome you have, and each outcome should occur about as often as the others (give or take about 10). Now do the same for two six-sided dice, and you'll see that 7 will occur a lot more often than 2 or 12.

With 1d200 it's also easier to keep track of how abundant a subrace is. Let's say that a certain race is roughly 20% of the population, then you give them 60-99 (because 40 is 20% of 200). We also want one subgroup and another subgroup to be twice as abundant as a third subgroup, so we give the first subgroup 60-75, the second subgroup 76-91, and the third subgroup 92-99.

At level 1, a character has the maximum of their hit die, plus the Constitution modifier as hit points. So for instance, a spellcaster has a d6 for hit die. So they'll have 6 plus the Constitution modifier. If we assume they have a Constitution score of 11 (for a +0 bonus), they'll have 6+0=6 hit points. Similarly, a melee fighter will have 12 plus the Constitution modifier in hit points. If they have a Constitution of 14 (a +2 bonus), they'll have 14 hit points.

For every next level in that same class, you gain hit die plus the Constitution modifier in hit points. So those same spellcaster and melee fighter will, at level 2, have 6+0 (from level 1) +1d6+0 hit points and 12+2 (also from level 1)+1d12+2 hit points. If the spellcaster rolls a 6, and the melee fighter a 1, they end up with 12 and 17 hit points. As an alternative, you can pick the average, rounded up. So the spellcaster will have 6+4=10 hit points, and the melee fighter 12+2+7+2=23 hit points.

Sure, anyone among those 150 million could be president. But first, you would need to want to be president. So that should cut the total down a bit. Next is the fact that campaigning costs a lot of money. You've got to get flyers designed and printed, get media coverage, talk to people, give speeches, etc. And all of this in multiple states. This is going to cost a lot. But this can be remedied by asking like-minded people for a bit of cash to show their support. Let's say 50 bucks annually. And now we've got parties.

In reality, each person is his own party, as two people don't share the exact views on everything, but you can probably find a lot of people that share enough of your views. So let's say we have 4 parties: Extreme Right (ER), Moderate Right (MR), Moderate Left (ML), and Extreme Left (EL). First, we assume that everybody votes for who they think is best, and because ML has campaigned better, or had better views, they win. This means that the rest of the parties aren't happy, but EL is at least satisfied, because at least it's another left-wing winner. But ER is not happy. Just like EL can tolerate an ML winner, they could tolerate an MR winner. So maybe next time, some of them are going to vote MR, in order to not 'waste their vote'. And MR knows this, so they might adjust their policies a bit so that they'll attract even more of those voters. The next elections, MR wins because of this practice, so ML does the same. And after a while, you've got two large parties, and a couple of smaller ones. And as the smaller parties start getting smaller, people are going to more easily think votes for those parties are wasted.

Add to this that a two-party system can easily lead to anti-voting, that is voting *against* a candidate: A is bad, but B is terrible, so I'm going to vote for B. And if there isn't mandatory voting, then it also leads to people not voting because none of the candidates represent them: I don't want either of these candidates to win, but there isn't another choice, so I won't vote. But since only votes are counted, this doesn't matter. If only three people vote, and two vote for A, and one for B, A still wins (ok, not exactly because of the electoral system, but that's another thing entirely).

Of course, as a party, you're going to pick only one candidate. Because if your opponent has one, you have two, and two-thirds of the voters would vote for you, but that's split evenly, your opponent might win (each candidate gets a third of the votes). And then you've lost.

So how are you going to pick this candidate? You can draw lots from the pool of party members, or from the pool of people that want to run. Or the party leader(s) can pick someone. Or, since we're in a democracy (and don't give me the "the United States is a republic, not a democracy" argument, since they aren't mutually exclusive. Look it up.), we can ask our members who to pick. And, as far as I know, one of the major parties has a mix of these last two. The members vote for who they want in office, and the state delegates then vote accordingly. For instance, a state has three delegates, and 2/3 vote for candidate A, then 2 of the three delegates also vote for candidate A. But there are also so-called super delegates (SD), who are unrestricted in their votes. These SDs were rather controversial in the latest elections. One candidate had about 43% of the popular votes, but only 7% of the SDs voted for him. This meant that a lot of his supporters were mad at the party and didn't vote in the presidential elections, or voted for the opposing candidate (see again the anti-vote). And he was also gracious in defeat and acknowledged the other candidate as the nominee, and didn't run as independent.

The other major party, on the other hand, has a more direct way of choosing their candidate. Even their 'super-delegates' (not called that, but similar) have to vote for their state's candidate. This can lead to a populist candidate winning the vote, and in fact, before 1980, this was also the case in the other major party. But after a loss in the presidential election, the system of SDs was instituted to prevent this.

Do note that in the end, neither of these organizations are required by law to pick those candidates. They could, in theory, disregard their members and pick whoever. But this would be very bad, since you'll lose a lot of voters that way: my party didn't listen to me when asked who I wanted, why would they listen to anything else I say?

So that's how you can get these two candidates. As to how one candidate has won, that is, as far as I know, partly because of the Electoral College (the other candidate had the popular vote), and partly because a lot of voters from the opposing party didn't go to vote, or voted against that candidate.

This is one of the easiest formulas to understand. It starts from the fact that many functions can be described as an infinite sum, called a Taylor series. The nth term in this series is:

f^((n)) (a)(x-a)^n /n!

We're trying to get the value of the function f(x) around point a. Here f^((n)) is the nth derivative of f and n! is the factorial. By summing these terms for n going from 0 to infinity, we get the exact function. From now on, I'm going to identify a series with its nth term. So for example:

* sin(x) -> (-1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!
* 1/(1-x) -> x^n
* e^x -> x^n /n!
* atan(x) -> (-1)^n x^(2n+1) /(2n+1)

The series expansion can be used to approximate pretty much any irrational numbers. For instance, the nth root of m, with n and m as integers. This is just calculating f(m)=m^(1/n). But the more interesting numbers are those such as e, pi, ln(2), log(e)... Some of those are obviously a function (ln(2), log(e)), but for instance pi and e aren't. So if we can define a function so that for a certain value x f(x) equals that function, we're back in business.

And it just so happens that e^1=e, so if we compute the sum of 1/n!, we should get e as a result. Similarly, atan(1)=pi/4, so (-1)^n 4/(2n+1) should equal pi.
